items.stem: Which term describes crime that crosses national borders and is organised through global networks?

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “global criminal economy”, and give one example.
items.answer: Castells’s term for the worldwide network of illegal trade worth trillions of dollars. Example: arms, drugs, people and money laundering.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (Castells’s term for the worldwide network of illegal trade worth trillions of dollars); 1 mark for a relevant example such as arms, drugs, people and money laundering. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “human trafficking” and “cybercrime”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Human trafficking: the movement of people by force, fraud or deception for exploitation (e.g. people forced into labour or sex work abroad). Cybercrime: crime carried out using computers and the internet (e.g. online fraud, hacking and identity theft).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Police in Riyadh trace a fraud ring that stole money from thousands of people online; the servers were in one country, the organisers in another and the victims in twenty more. Suggest how a functionalist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Functionalism: crime reveals weaknesses in social regulation; global crime grows where anomie and weak controls exist, and responses reaffirm shared values.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A factory near Seoul legally pours waste chemicals into a river, killing fish and harming villagers’ health downstream. Explain how a functionalist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: crime reveals weaknesses in social regulation; global crime grows where anomie and weak controls exist, and responses reaffirm shared values.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of official statistics for studying reported cybercrime in different countries.
items.answer: Strengths: regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified; they cover very large numbers of people, often a whole population, so they are representative. Limitations: they show patterns but not the meanings or reasons behind them; they are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying reported cybercrime in different countries but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.answer: Transformationalism: globalisation creates networks that criminals use; crime and control are reshaped across borders (Castells). items.stem: The table shows cybercrimes recorded by police in one country. Table: cybercrimes recorded by police in a country (thousands) | 2018 | 2023. Online fraud | 57 | 90. Hacking | 10 | 20. Identity theft | 22 | 32. (a) Calculate the gap between Identity theft and Hacking in 2018 and in 2023, and state whether it narrowed or widened. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that cybercrime is increasing rapidly.
items.answer: (a) 2018: 12 thousand offences; 2023: 12 thousand offences; the gap stayed the same. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Online fraud, Hacking, Identity theft; Online fraud had the highest figure for 2023. Criminals use cheaper and more sophisticated tools. Qualifications: Most cybercrime is unreported; changes may reflect recording practices or awareness; offenders and victims may be in other countries. The data also come from official statistics of 3 offences in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each gap (12 and 12); 1 mark for “stayed the same”. [3] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “reflexivity”? Give one example.
items.answer: The process by which individuals and institutions constantly monitor and reflect on risks and change their behaviour. Example: people changing diets after health warnings.

items.stem: Distinguish between “ontological insecurity” and “reflexivity”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Ontological insecurity: a feeling of uncertainty and anxiety about the world and one’s place in it (e.g. anxiety about climate change and job loss). Reflexivity: the process by which individuals and institutions constantly monitor and reflect on risks and change their behaviour (e.g. people changing diets after health warnings).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Residents of a poor district in Seoul live next to a waste incinerator, while wealthier residents can afford to move away from polluted areas. Suggest how an interactionist sociologist might explain this.

items.stem: After a nuclear power accident in a neighbouring country, people in Hanoi stop buying local vegetables, demand radiation tests and protest against building a new power station. Explain how a late modern sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Late modernity: society is a risk society: manufactured global risks lead to reflexivity, as people and institutions monitor and respond to risks (Beck, Giddens).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using content analysis to research how newspapers report climate change.
items.answer: Strengths: media content from different decades can be compared to measure change; it allows representations to be compared over time or between different media. Limitations: counting images or words may miss their deeper meaning and context; coding categories reflect the researcher’s own interpretation, so different coders may disagree. Theory: content analysis is favoured by positivist (quantitative content analysis) or interpretivist (qualitative content analysis) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how newspapers report climate change but best combined with another method such as structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: A survey of 1200 adults in Lima asked how worried they were about global risks. Table: adults “very worried” about each risk (%) | Lowest income group | Highest income group. Climate change | 61% | 67%. Pandemics | 59% | 61%. Nuclear accidents | 26% | 17%. (a) Calculate the difference between Pandemics and Nuclear accidents for Lowest income group and for Highest income group, and state for which of these the difference is larger. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that concern about global risks is shared across social classes, as Beck suggests.
items.answer: (a) Lowest income group: 33 percentage points; Highest income group: 44 percentage points; the difference is larger for Highest income group. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure is higher for Highest income group than for Lowest income group among Climate change, Pandemics; the figure is lower for Highest income group than for Lowest income group among Nuclear accidents; Climate change had the highest figure for Highest income group. Lower-income groups face more immediate everyday risks. Qualifications: Concern is not the same as exposure; poorer groups may face greater actual risk; “very worried” may be interpreted differently. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 1200 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each difference (33 and 44); 1 mark for the correct comparison. [3] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: A research team is investigating how people perceive environmental risks. Evaluate the use of structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: trained interviewers can survey a large, representative sample in a standard way; response rates are usually higher than for postal questionnaires because the interviewer is present. Limitations: they are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid; the interview is an artificial social encounter, so answers may not reflect real behaviour. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how people perceive environmental risks but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using unstructured interviews to research how activists use social media.
items.answer: Strengths: they allow people to explain the meanings they give to their experiences in their own words; they produce rich, detailed qualitative data that gives verstehen (an empathetic understanding). Limitations: they cannot measure patterns across a large population because only a few people can be interviewed; each interview is unique, so it is hard to repeat and the data is less reliable. Theory: unstructured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how activists use social media but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using participant observation to research how activists use social media.
items.answer: Strengths: it reveals the meanings and labels that shape interaction as it happens; it is often the only way to study small or closed groups in depth. Limitations: it cannot measure the extent of a pattern across a whole society; studies are small-scale and impossible to repeat exactly, so findings are unreliable and hard to generalise. Theory: participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how activists use social media but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using self-completion questionnaires to research the experiences of victims of trafficking.
items.answer: Strengths: anonymity may encourage respondents to admit sensitive or embarrassing behaviour they would not reveal face to face; they can reach a large, geographically spread sample quickly and cheaply, so findings can be generalised. Limitations: pre-set answers cannot capture the subjective meanings people attach to their experiences; they measure what people say they do, not what they actually do. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the experiences of victims of trafficking but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of semi-structured interviews for studying the experiences of victims of trafficking.

Theory: semi-structured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative and quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the experiences of victims of trafficking but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes the process by which individuals and institutions constantly monitor and reflect on risks and change their behaviour?
items.answer: Reflexivity
items.markingKey: Reflexivity: the process by which individuals and institutions constantly monitor and reflect on risks and change their behaviour. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “boomerang effect”.
items.answer: Beck’s idea that risks eventually affect those who produced them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: Beck’s idea that risks eventually affect those who produced them. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between natural and manufactured risks, using an example of each.
items.answer: Natural risks come from nature (e.g. earthquakes, drought); manufactured risks come from human activity and technology (e.g. nuclear accidents, climate change).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each meaning; 1 mark each example. [4]

items.stem: Ana surveyed 1200 adults about risks. The results by income group are shown below. Table: adults “very worried” about each risk (%) | Lowest income group | Highest income group. Climate change | 65% | 74%. Pandemics | 55% | 62%. Nuclear accidents | 29% | 25%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between Lowest income group and Highest income group for Pandemics (Highest income group minus Lowest income group)?
items.answer: +7 percentage points
items.markingKey: 62 − 55 = +7 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: A sociologist in Seoul wants to research how people perceive environmental risks. Explain one strength of using case studies for this research.
items.answer: They give a detailed, in-depth picture of one group, institution or community.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of how people perceive environmental risks. [2]

items.stem: A research team is investigating how newspapers report climate change. Evaluate the use of content analysis for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: media content from different decades can be compared to measure change; quantitative content analysis using a coding sheet can be repeated by another researcher, so it is reliable. Limitations: coding categories reflect the researcher’s own interpretation, so different coders may disagree; counting images or words may miss their deeper meaning and context. Theory: content analysis is favoured by positivist (quantitative content analysis) or interpretivist (qualitative content analysis) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how newspapers report climate change but best combined with another method such as official statistics (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of structured interviews for studying how newspapers report climate change.
items.answer: Strengths: trained interviewers can survey a large, representative sample in a standard way; response rates are usually higher than for postal questionnaires because the interviewer is present. Limitations: the fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth; the interviewer’s presence may produce interviewer bias or socially desirable answers. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how newspapers report climate change but best combined with another method such as content analysis (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: Which term describes a social movement that organises across national borders on global issues?
items.answer: Global social movement
items.markingKey: Global social movement: a social movement that organises across national borders on global issues. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “New social movements focus mainly on improving wages for factory workers.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. They focus mainly on identity, lifestyle and global issues such as the environment and human rights.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: Explain Klein’s argument that the anti-globalisation movement challenges the power of global brands and corporations, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Klein showed how activists exposed sweatshops and corporate power. Criticism: Critics argue such movements have achieved few structural changes.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Neo-Marxism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: A national survey of 450 young people aged 18-24 produced the results below. Table: young people aged 18-24 who reported each activity (%) | 2010 | 2022. Signed an online petition | 21% | 48%. Joined a street protest | 5% | 14%. Voted in the last national election | 57% | 53%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Signed an online petition change between 2010 and 2022?
items.answer: +27 percentage points
items.markingKey: 48 − 21 = +27 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: School students in Cairo join a global climate strike organised online; on the same day, similar strikes take place in over 100 countries. Explain how a sceptical sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Globalisation scepticism: states remain the key decision-makers; global movements still need to persuade national governments to act.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using non-participant observation to research why young people join climate protests.
items.answer: Strengths: children can be observed in classrooms or playgrounds without having to answer questions; the researcher stays detached, so is less likely to “go native” and can record more objectively. Limitations: the presence of an observer may change behaviour (the Hawthorne effect); observation schedules impose the researcher’s categories on behaviour. Theory: non-participant observation is favoured by both positivist and interpretivist (depending on how structured it is) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying why young people join climate protests but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]
